title: Detecting basis-dependent hardware errors through spatio-temporal quantum steering
authors: Hsiang-Wei Huang, Kuo-Feng Chiu, Yi-Te Huang, Jhen-Dong Lin, Tse-Ming Chen, Yueh-Nan Chen
abstract: Spatio-temporal quantum steering provides a framework for benchmarking the nonclassicality of general quantum state transfer processes. A central diagnostic is the no-signaling-in-time (NSIT) condition, whose violation can indicate basis-dependent hardware errors. However, finite measurement statistics may also yield apparent violations, thereby obscuring the detection of basis-dependent hardware errors. To address this, we construct a statistical hypothesis test under the null hypothesis that NSIT violations arise solely from statistical fluctuations. Combining the statistical properties of NSIT violation under the null hypothesis with Chebyshev's inequality, we obtain a distribution-free upper bound on the $p$-value without parametric assumptions. We apply this method to two examples. For a single-qubit state-transfer experiment on a superconducting processor, we observe several instances that the NSIT violation is observed and the null hypothesis is simultaneously rejected by a small $p$-value, providing statistical evidence of basis-dependent hardware errors. For a seven-qubit Hayden-Preskill teleportation protocol on IonQ devices, the null hypothesis is also rejected even when the average fidelity exceeds the classical threshold, while the associated nonclassicality measure vanishes. Our results highlight the necessity of statistical hypothesis testing for detecting basis-dependent errors in near-term quantum devices.
summary: This work introduces a statistical hypothesis test based on the No-Signaling-In-Time (NSIT) condition to diagnose basis-dependent errors in quantum state transfer. By using Chebyshev's inequality, the authors distinguish genuine hardware flaws from mere statistical noise across superconducting and trapped-ion platforms. The findings emphasize that advanced statistical testing is necessary for reliable benchmarking of current quantum devices.
main_problem: The paper addresses the critical need for robust methods to detect basis-dependent hardware errors during quantum state transfer (QST) processes.
main_result: By employing statistical hypothesis testing on the violation of the No-Signaling-In-Time (NSIT) condition, the authors provided statistical evidence of intrinsic hardware errors in superconducting and trapped-ion platforms.
method: They constructed a distribution-free upper bound on the p-value using Chebyshev's inequality to test the null hypothesis that observed NSIT violations are merely due to finite measurement statistics.
model_or_system: The study uses the spatio-temporal quantum steering (STS) framework applied to qubit systems, testing protocols like single-qubit state transfer and seven-qubit Hayden-Preskill teleportation on superconducting and trapped-ion devices.
key_observables: No-signaling-in-time violation measure ($D$), statistical p-value upper bound ($p_U$), and Spatio-Temporal Steering Robustness (STSR).
important_parameters: Superconducting processor parameters, IonQ device fidelity ($F_{avg}$), and the significance level $\alpha$.
main_assumptions: The statistical test assumes measurements are independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.), which is noted as a limitation for real-world devices.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the STS framework, hypothesis testing on $D$ vs time, and device schematics for superconducting processors and teleportation circuits.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the diagnostic tool (NSIT violation), develops the statistical test using Chebyshev's inequality to handle finite statistics, and then applies this method sequentially to two distinct hardware platforms (superconducting and trapped-ion).
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous, statistically grounded methodology for benchmarking near-term quantum hardware beyond simple fidelity metrics, which is crucial for advancing fault-tolerant quantum computation.
